Related Work 2.1. Vision-and-Language Navigation Benefiting from deep learning technologies [16, 19, 34, 35, 37–47], early methods enhanced VLN via learn- ing [2, 7, 8, 10, 12, 56] and data augmentation [9, 31]. Traditional training-based methods, such as Speaker- Follower [9], EnvDrop [31], and PREVALENT [10], employed Seq2Seq [30] or Transformer-based architec- tures [32]. However, scarcity of instructions and limited scene diversity hindered robust navigation policies, result- ing in poor generalization. Foundation models have introduced two paradigms for VLN [6, 27, 29, 53]. The first centers on post-training adap- tation [15, 21, 49, 52, 54], where models are fine-tuned on domain-specific datasets. For instance, NaviLLM [54] uni- fies diverse navigation tasks through schema-based instruc- tions and multi-view fusion. These methods achieve strong in-domain results but require significant computation and struggle with generalization. The second paradigm explores training-free methods [5, 6, 22, 26, 55] exploiting zero-shot reasoning without task-specific tuning. NavGPT [55] con- verts panoramic scenes into textual descriptions for GPT-4- based action prediction, while AO-Planner [6] employs vi- sual affordance prompts using SAM for waypoint planning. 2.2. Perception and Contextual Reasoning Despite the remarkable progress brought by foundation model-based VLN paradigms [29, 50], these existing ap- proaches [49, 55] still encounter two major challenges in perception and contextual reasoning. (1) Perception. Most existing methods [29, 49, 50] rely heavily on extensive vi- sual inputs, such as panoramic observations [49, 55], multi- view images [29, 50, 54], or continuous video streams [51]. For example, NaviLLM [54] processes multi-view inputs via Vision Transformers and fuses them for holistic scene understanding. While such designs capture rich environ- mental information, they uniformly process dense visual to- kens, resulting in visual token inflation. This passive per- ception paradigm suggests the need for proactive acqui- sition that selectively gathers instruction-relevant observa- tions. (2) Contextual Reasoning. Existing methods often exhibit unfocused reasoning by treating historical contexts indiscriminately [6, 49, 55]. They typically store all past information in the form of historical frames [49, 54], tex- tual descriptions [6, 55], or graph representations [5, 52]. Although approaches such as NavFoM’s [50] token-based sampling and OpenNav’s [26] multi-granularity dynamic memory (MGDM) attempt to manage memory, they still rely on recency-based heuristics or fixed policies, failing to dynamically assess the semantic importance of way- points. For instance, NavFoM’s [50] BATS allocates to- kens based on temporal proximity rather than semantic rele- vance, hindering retrieval of critical waypoints during back- tracking. These limitations motivate ProFocus, which in- troduces value-driven waypoint prioritization to enable fo- cused reasoning over historical contexts. 3. Methodology 3.1. Overview Problem formulation.
